Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
As he wiped down the counter for what felt like the hundredth time that shift, 19-year-old Ryder couldn't shake the feeling of unease that had been building up inside him since the hurricane hit his hometown last year. The howling winds and torrential rains had torn through the small community, leaving destruction in its wake. Ryder's family had lost their home, and he had lost something far more valuable – a sense of security. The memories of that night still haunted him. He would see flashes of debris-filled streets, shattered windows, and uprooted trees. The smell of wet earth and ozone would transport him back to the midst of the storm, his heart racing with terror. Ryder's mind was flooded with vivid images – the sound of shattering glass, the feeling of being helpless as the winds howled on. As he struggled to come to terms with what had happened, Ryder began to notice changes in himself. He used to be a happy-go-lucky guy, always cracking jokes and making his friends laugh. Now, he felt like a stranger in his own skin. Simple interactions left him feeling anxious, so he started rehearsing conversations before they even happened. What if someone asked about the hurricane? How would he respond without breaking down? Ryder's avoidance strategies soon became a way of life. He stopped hanging out with friends, fearing that they might bring up the traumatic event. He turned down invitations to social gatherings, opting instead for solitary nights at home. Even at work, he found himself dodging conversations about the weather or current events, terrified that someone might mention the hurricane. As the months went by, Ryder's suppression of thoughts became a reflex. He pushed away memories of the storm, trying hard not to think about it. But the more he tried to suppress them, the more they seemed to seep into his daily life. The smell of rain would bring back the terror; a strong gust of wind would make him jump. Ryder's self-perception began to unravel. He felt like he had permanently changed for the worse, that he was no longer the carefree person he once was. His friends and family noticed the difference too – they would comment on how withdrawn he had become. Ryder felt lost, unsure of who he was anymore or what the future held. As the anniversary of the hurricane approached, Ryder's anxiety reached a boiling point. He found himself questioning whether he could ever go back to being his old self. The thought sent him into a spiral of despair – would he be forever trapped in this cycle of fear and avoidance? One evening, as he was closing up the restaurant, Ryder realized that he couldn't keep living like this. He needed help to confront the demons that had taken over his life. With a sense of trepidation, he picked up the phone and made an appointment with a therapist, hoping against hope that someone could guide him back to a place of peace and recognition – back to himself.
